Directs the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy to designate a senior civilian official, at or above the Assistant Secretary level, to develop and oversee compliance with Defense Department policy on civilian casualties from U.S. military operations. The statute lists what that policy must cover, from recording strikes to acknowledging harm and offering payments.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 115-232](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/232){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 10 U.S.C. 134 note](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/10/134?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 936(a): a senior civilian official in the Office of the Secretary of Defense develops, coordinates, and oversees compliance with civilian casualty policy.
- Sec. 936(b)(1), (4): uniform standards across combatant commands for recording kinetic strikes and for reviewing and investigating civilian casualty allegations.
- Sec. 936(b)(3): public means, including an internet-based mechanism, for submitting allegations of civilian casualties.
- Sec. 936(b)(5): uniform processes for acknowledging responsibility, including for people first believed to be combatants and later found to be non-combatants, and for offering ex gratia payments or other assistance.
- Sec. 936(c): coordination with chiefs of mission and the State Department on civilian harm.

## Why it matters

This section is the statutory root of the Department's civilian harm mitigation and response program, which was set out in a 2022 action plan and a 2023 Defense Department instruction (DoDI 3000.17). The [Civilian Protection Center of Excellence](cp-coe-2022.qmd) and the allegation procedures added to the [ex gratia authority](ex-gratia-2019.qmd) build on it, and the public [annual report](civcas-report-2017.qmd) measures its results.

## Current status

In force. A June 2026 analysis of a Defense Department Inspector General evaluation reported that civilian harm staff had been cut to about a tenth of their earlier size in 2025 and 2026. It also reported that the Department and the Inspector General disagreed over what the statute requires of the designated senior official. Check current status.

[Last checked November 10, 2026.]{.checked}
